question: A singer and a violinist play the same G, 196 Hz. Same pitch, so what makes them sound nothing alike?
answer: The recipe of harmonics. Both make a stack of multiples of 196 Hz, so both repeat 196 times a second: that is the pitch. What differs is how loud each harmonic is. A violin's wooden body boosts fixed bands; a singer's throat and mouth reshape theirs with every vowel.
move: Two things that measure the same can still be made differently.
ask: Which two things do I lump together because one number matches?

scene.hint: A G at 196 Hz, the violin's lowest string, from three harmonics. Change the recipe.

moments.name: Pure tone
moments.text: One sine wave, near what a tuning fork makes: plain, and hard to place.

moments.name: Full stack
moments.text: Every harmonic strong: the bright buzz of a bowed string before the wood shapes it.

moments.name: Top only
moments.text: Only higher harmonics: thin and nasal. The pitch is still 196 Hz.

moments.name: Low two
moments.text: Only the two lowest: soft and round, nearer a flute or a hum.

reference: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments, 2nd edn, Springer, 1998 (violin body resonances); Sundberg, The Science of the Singing Voice, Northern Illinois University Press, 1987 (formants)
